segments: Six years before the attack, August 1939. The world stands on the brink of the most destructive war
in human history, but the greatest threat is still invisible, hidden in equations and physics
laboratories. At the urging of his colleague Leo Szilard, Albert Einstein sends a letter to
President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Its warning is chilling. Nazi Germany may already be developing
an entirely new kind of bomb, one powered by a nuclear chain reaction. The scientists warned
that a single bomb dropped from an airplane could destroy an entire city and the surrounding area.
Einstein urges Roosevelt to begin America's own research. The letter sets something in motion
that will forever change history, warfare, and the very nature of human fear.
Three years before the attack, August 1942. The U.S. government officially launches the
Manhattan Project, the largest, most expensive, and most secretive research program in the world.
Under General Leslie Groves and brilliant physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, a secret town rises from the
New Mexico desert. Across the country, enormous industrial facilities take shape. Oak Ridge enriches
uranium. Hanford produces plutonium. More than 130,000 people work on the project, but only a
select few know its ultimate purpose. Most workers simply monitor instruments without understanding what
they are helping produce. The resources of an entire nation are mobilized to harness the energy
inside the atom before anyone else can. The race is on, though Germany's nuclear program, as the Americans
will later discover, is hopelessly behind. One year before the attack, summer 1944. The Pacific War has
become a relentless slaughter. American aircraft are already devastating Japanese cities with incendiary
bombing raids. Tokyo has been reduced to ashes. Hundreds of thousands of civilians are dying.
Meanwhile, scientists at Los Alamos now believe an atomic bomb is only a matter of time.
A special committee is formed to select targets. The list includes Kyoto, Hiroshima, Yokohama, Kokura,
and Niigata. The criteria are specific. The cities must have military or industrial importance,
and they must be relatively undamaged by conventional bombing so the effects of the new weapon can be
measured. Secretary of War Henry Stimson will later personally remove Kyoto, Japan's ancient capital,
from the list. He recognizes its cultural importance and wants to avoid creating lasting Japanese hatred
after the war. Hiroshima, a major industrial center and military port, becomes the primary target.
One month before the attack. The Jornada del Muerto Desert, New Mexico. Before dawn, a flash brighter than a
thousand suns lights up the landscape. This is Trinity, the first nuclear explosion in human history.
A fireball rises into the sky, becoming an enormous mushroom cloud of smoke and radioactive dust.
Sand beneath the blast melts into greenish glass. Watching the apocalyptic scene from a bunker,
Oppenheimer recalls a line from the Bhagavad Gita, an ancient Hindu scripture,
Now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds. A few days later, President Harry Truman, who succeeded
Roosevelt after his death, receives word that the test was successful. The United States now possesses
the most powerful weapon on earth. The Allies issue the Potsdam Declaration, demanding Japan's
unconditional surrender and warning of prompt and utter destruction if it refuses. Japan's government
dismisses the warning, treating it as another bluff. One week before the attack. Under strict secrecy,
the heavy cruiser USS Indianapolis delivers the uranium core and other key components of the first bomb
to Tinian in the Pacific. The island has become the world's largest military air base. From here, B-29
heavy bombers regularly launch raids against Japan. Inside an air-conditioned assembly building,
technicians put together a weapon roughly 10 feet long and weighing more than 8,800 pounds. Its name is
Little Boy. Meanwhile, crews of the specially formed 509th composite group practice dropping heavy dummy bombs
and making a sharp 155 degree turn, the maneuver that will give them a chance to escape the blast.
24 hours before the attack. August 5, 1945. Colonel Paul Tibbetts orders his mother's name painted on the nose of his B-29,
Enola Gay. At the evening briefing, the crews are told they will drop a bomb of extraordinary destructive power,
a weapon that could end the war. No one uses the word atomic, but the tension is unmistakable. Pilots receive cyanide capsules in
case they are captured. Around midnight, Little Boy is carefully loaded into the bomb bay. Navy Captain
William Parsons, the mission's weapons officer, decides to complete the arming process in the air.
The heavily loaded bomber faces a dangerous takeoff, and he wants to prevent an accidental detonation if it
crashes. One hour before the attack. The aircraft has been airborne for several hours. Parsons has climbed
into the cold bomb bay and inserted the propellant charges designed to drive one piece of uranium into
another, starting the chain reaction. The bomb is armed. The plane approaches Japan. Weather reconnaissance
aircraft have gone ahead to check conditions over the targets. Meanwhile, Hiroshima wakes up. It is an
ordinary hot summer morning, and the city is busy with wartime activity. The streets are crowded. Thousands of
teenage students have been mobilized to tear down wooden buildings in the city center, creating fire
breaks against incendiary raids. None of them is looking up. An air raid warning triggered by an
earlier aircraft has already been lifted. The weather plane's straight flush sends Enola Gay a brief
message. Clear skies over Hiroshima. Visibility is excellent. At 8.14 a.m., the bomber begins its final
approach at more than 31,000 feet. The city lies clearly visible below. Through his bombsite, bombardier
Thomas Faraby picks out the T-shaped Aoi Bridge in central Hiroshima, an unmistakable landmark. The bomb
bay doors rumble open. The crew puts on dark protective goggles to shield their eyes from the flash.
The attack. Little boy, weighing nearly 9,000 pounds, drops from its release mechanism. Suddenly lighter,
the aircraft jumps upward. Tibbetts immediately banks into a steep turn, trying to gain speed and put as
much distance as possible between the plane and the bomb. The bomb falls for 43 seconds. Its automatic
sensors track its altitude. At roughly 1,900 feet above the ground, it detonates. For an instant, a new sun
appears above Hiroshima. Temperatures at the center of the explosion reach several million degrees.
Directly beneath it, people, trees, birds in flight, and wooden homes instantly vaporize into plasma.
Dark silhouettes remain on walls where people had been sitting seconds earlier. The flash is so bright
that it blinds people miles away. A fraction of a second after the flash comes the blast wave. Superheated
air expands into a dense wall moving faster than sound. It tears the city apart. Reinforced concrete
buildings crumple like cardboard boxes. Wooden neighborhoods are swept away. Behind the blast
comes a powerful inward rush of air, feeding the fires that have erupted everywhere. Above the
devastated city, a huge purple-gray mushroom cloud of smoke, dust, and radioactive debris climbs more than
nine miles into the sky, blotting out the morning sun. One minute later. The first shockwave catches
Enola Gay. The enormous bomber shudders as though struck by a giant sledgehammer. Co-pilot Robert
Lewis looks out at the churning mass of fire and dust where a city stood moments before. My god, what have we
done? Hiroshima, as it existed a minute earlier, is gone. Across nearly five square miles, everything has been
destroyed. Within roughly a mile and a quarter of the point beneath the blast, anyone without the
protection of thick concrete walls is dead or dying. Tens of thousands have been killed in the first
second. One hour later. The city becomes an inferno. Thousands of separate fires merge into a firestorm,
drawing air in from every direction and driving the flames higher. The heat in the streets is unbearable.
Survivors emerge from the wreckage like ghosts. In shock, they stumble forward with their arms extended,
strips of burned skin hanging from them. The flash has seared their clothing into their bodies. Many faces are so
swollen that their features are unrecognizable. Soon, rain begins falling from the radioactive cloud. It is black and
sticky, carrying soot, ash, and lethal radioactive contamination. Desperate with thirst, people open their mouths to drink it,
unaware that they are swallowing a poison that will kill them within hours.
24 hours after the Hiroshima attack, Japan's military leadership in Tokyo cannot understand what has happened.
All communication with Hiroshima has stopped. Railway telegraph operators report that lines north of the city are down.
The general staff sends an aircraft to investigate. From nearly a hundred miles away, the pilot can already see the enormous cloud of smoke.
Below it lies a seemingly endless expanse of burned ruins.
President Truman announces to the world by radio that the United States has used an atomic bomb.
Unless Japan surrenders, he promises a rain of ruin from the air.
Many Japanese military leaders refuse to believe the Americans have more than one such weapon.
Japan does not surrender.
Three days later, hours before the second attack.
At dawn, the Soviet Union fulfills its commitment at the Yalta Conference, declaring war on Japan and launching a massive offensive in Manchuria.
The Japanese Empire's strategic position becomes hopeless.
Meanwhile, on Tinian, the Americans rush to prepare a second strike.
An approaching typhoon has moved the mission forward by two days.
A B-29 named Boxcar takes off, piloted by Major Charles Sweeney.
In its bomb bay is Fat Man, a plutonium implosion bomb, more complex and more powerful than the weapon dropped on Hiroshima.
The primary target is Kokura, home to a major military arsenal.
From the beginning, things go wrong.
A faulty fuel pump makes the reserve fuel inaccessible.
When Boxcar reaches Kokura, clouds and smoke from fires in a nearby city obscure the target.
The crew makes three passes, but the bombardier cannot identify his aiming point.
Anti-aircraft guns begin finding the aircraft's range.
Japanese fighters take off to intercept it.
Fuel is running low.
Sweeney decides to head for the alternate target, Nagasaki.
The attack on Nagasaki.
11 AM.
Nagasaki is a major port city spread through valleys between mountains.
Boxcar approaches with barely enough fuel left to reach Okinawa.
Nagasaki, too, is hidden beneath clouds.
The city is visible on radar, but the crew is under orders to identify the target visually before releasing the bomb.
Sweeney is almost out of options.
Sweeney turns away and drop the weapon into the ocean, or attempt an emergency landing on Okinawa with it still aboard.
Then, a break appears in the clouds.
Bombardier Kermit Behan spots a stadium and industrial buildings in the Urakami Valley.
Fat Man leaves the bomb bay.
It explodes roughly 1,600 feet above Urakami, a district with a large Christian community.
The blast is more powerful than Hiroshima's, with a yield equivalent to about 21,000 tons of TNT.
The fireball instantly engulfs Urakami Cathedral, the largest Catholic cathedral in Asia, along with Mitsubishi factories, schools, and hospitals.
The surrounding mountains shield the rest of Nagasaki, preventing the blast from spreading across the city as evenly as it did in Hiroshima.
But within the valley, the destruction is total.
Tens of thousands more lives end in an instant.
24 hours after the Nagasaki attack, two cities have been devastated.
Soviet tanks are advancing rapidly across Manchuria.
In Tokyo, the Supreme War Council remains in continuous session.
Its members are evenly divided.
Half favor unconditional surrender.
The others, including the army minister and army chief of staff, demand a final battle on Japan's home islands,
even at the cost of millions of civilian lives.
For the first time in Japan's modern history, Emperor Hirohito intervenes directly in the debate.
Breaking the monarch's customary silence, he instructs the government to accept the Potsdam Declaration,
with one condition, preserving imperial authority.
One week later, across Japan, people gather around radios.
Most have never heard their emperor's voice.
Through the static comes a recording of his speech.
His formal, archaic language is difficult to follow, and many listeners do not immediately understand.
But the central message becomes clear.
The war has turned against Japan.
The enemy has begun using a new and exceptionally cruel bomb,
a weapon of immeasurable destructive power that is taking countless innocent lives.
Continuing the war would destroy the Japanese nation.
Japan surrenders.
World War II is over.
In Tokyo, people weep with despair and relief.
In New York, London, and Moscow, crowds celebrate.
In the ruins of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, people keep dying.
One month later, American occupation forces arrive in Japan.
The first Western journalists and scientists reach Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
What they find shocks the world.
An invisible killer is revealing itself.
Something doctors initially call Disease X.
People who survived the explosions without a scratch, helped clear rubble, and appeared healthy,
suddenly grow weak.
Their hair falls out.
Their gums bleed.
Dark red patches appear beneath their skin.
Fevers climb to 104 degrees Fahrenheit.
White blood cell counts collapse.
This is acute radiation sickness.
Radiation has damaged their bone marrow and cells.
Doctors can do little but watch patients deteriorate and die within days.
Weeks after the explosions, the death toll continues to climb.
Occupation authorities impose censorship, trying to conceal the extent of the radiation injuries.
One year later, the ruins of Hiroshima and Nagasaki are gradually being cleared.
People live in makeshift wooden shacks built from debris.
A new group emerges.
The Hibakusha.
Literally, people affected by the bomb.
They face rejection within their own society.
Employers hesitate to hire them.
Potential spouses turn them away, afraid of genetic damage or the mistaken belief that radiation exposure
is contagious.
Meanwhile, the world has changed irreversibly.
The Iron Curtain descends across Europe.
In the summer of 1946, the United States conducts Operation Crossroads at Bikini Atoll,
staging nuclear tests before the eyes of the world.
The Soviet Union accelerates its own atomic program.
The Cold War has begun.
The atomic bomb, introduced as a weapon to end a war,
becomes the defining fear of generations to come.
Humanity has taken itself hostage.
Eighty years later.
Today, Hiroshima and Nagasaki are thriving modern cities.
High-speed trains run through them.
Neon signs glow.
Their streets are full of life.
Time and human effort have erased the physical devastation.
But the memory remains.
At the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, damaged watches are forever stopped at 8.15.
There are burned children's school bags and shadows preserved on stone.
The total number of deaths from the blasts, fires, and long-term effects of radiation is estimated at more than 200,000 in Hiroshima and around 140,000 in Nagasaki.
Today, the world has more than 12,000 nuclear warheads.
Many are tens or hundreds of times more powerful than the bombs dropped on Japan.
Technology has advanced.
Guidance systems have become extraordinarily precise.
Weapons can reach their targets in minutes.
But their fundamental purpose remains unchanged.
Total indiscriminate destruction.
Every year, fewer hibakusha remain to tell their stories.
Throughout their lives, they have carried one message to the world,
hoping humanity has learned the lesson of August 1945.
It is inscribed on the cenotaph in Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Park.
Let all the souls here rest in peace, for we shall not repeat the evil.
We can only hope that, as a civilization, we are capable of keeping that promise.
